title: The Engineering of Gothic Cathedrals
intro: This passage examines how a cluster of structural innovations transformed the churches of medieval Europe and made possible their vast walls of colored glass.

paragraphs.text: The churches built in western Europe before the mid-twelfth century, in the style now called Romanesque, were massive, dimly lit structures whose thick walls carried the enormous downward thrust of their stone roofs. Because the semicircular arches and heavy barrel vaults that these buildings employed pushed outward as well as downward, the walls supporting them had to be thick and nearly unbroken, pierced by only small windows that would not weaken the load-bearing masonry. What later builders achieved, in the style that spread from the Île-de-France after about 1140 and came to be known as Gothic, was a fundamental redistribution of these forces—a rethinking of how weight could be gathered, channeled, and delivered to the ground—that allowed walls to be opened up as never before. The result was an architecture of height and light rather than mass, in which the wall, no longer the roof's sole support, could largely dissolve into glass.

At the heart of this transformation lay the pointed arch, a form borrowed from earlier Islamic precedents but exploited by Gothic masons with new purpose. A semicircular arch has a fixed height determined entirely by its width, so that arches spanning openings of different sizes rise to different heights; a pointed arch, by contrast, can be made steeper or shallower independently of its span, letting builders bring arches of unequal width to a common level. More important still was the way the pointed arch handled thrust: because its sides rise more steeply toward the apex, the force it transmits is directed more nearly straight downward, reducing the sideways push that had obliged Romanesque builders to rely on such ponderous walls. This single geometric adjustment, seemingly modest, made possible the tall interiors that define the style.

The pointed arch found its fullest expression in the ribbed vault, a ceiling in which slender stone arches are erected first as a framework and the intervening spaces, or webs, then filled with lighter masonry. This method concentrated the vault's weight onto the ribs, which carried it down to a few points rather than spreading it along a wall. Once the roof's weight had been gathered onto these points, however, the builders faced a new problem: the outward thrust delivered at the top of each pier still had to be resisted somewhere. ■ The solution was the flying buttress, a half-arch of stone reaching from the upper wall across the aisle roof to a freestanding external pier. ■ By carrying the vault's lateral thrust over open space and down into these external supports, the buttress relieved the walls of their structural burden almost entirely. ■ Freed in this way, the wall between the piers could be thinned, raised, and replaced by an expanse of window. ■ Cathedrals such as Beauvais pushed this logic to its limits, and the collapse of its choir vault in 1284 shows how near to failure the boldest builders ventured.

The walls these devices set free were filled with stained glass on a scale without precedent, and contemporaries understood this glazing as far more than decoration. The theologian Abbot Suger, whose rebuilding of the abbey church of Saint-Denis in the 1140s is often taken as the beginning of the style, wrote of how the colored light streaming through such windows could lift the mind from the material world toward the divine, an idea drawing on a tradition that equated God with light. Whether or not the ordinary worshiper grasped these associations, the effect was undeniable: an interior bathed in shifting reds and blues, its upper reaches seemingly weightless, presented an image of heaven that the older, fortress-like churches could not match. The glowing narrative scenes served a plainer function as well, instructing a largely illiterate population in scripture. Light was thus both a structural consequence of the new engineering and a carrier of meaning it was made to serve.

Yet no cathedral could rise on structural ingenuity alone, for these were among the most costly and protracted undertakings of the age. A single great church might take a century or more to complete, its construction spanning the working lives of several master masons and depending on a fragile flow of funds from bishops, cathedral chapters, patrons, and pilgrims' offerings. The masons themselves, organized into lodges that guarded the geometric knowledge on which their trade depended, moved from site to site as commissions allowed, so that a change of master or an interruption in revenue could alter a building's design in mid-course. That so many were nonetheless completed testifies not only to the technical mastery of their builders but to the extraordinary social and economic effort a medieval town would pour, over generations, into one monument of stone and glass.

glossary.def: the outward or downward pushing force exerted by an arch or vault
an arched ceiling or roof made of stone or brick
a stone support built against a wall to strengthen it

questions.stem: According to paragraph 1, why did Romanesque churches have thick walls with only small windows?
options: Their builders lacked access to large panes of colored glass.
Their rounded arches and barrel vaults pushed outward as well as downward.
Their designers wanted to keep the interiors dim for religious reasons.
Their stone roofs were lighter than those of later Gothic churches.
questions.explain: 原文：“Because the semicircular arches and heavy barrel vaults that these buildings employed pushed outward as well as downward, the walls supporting them had to be thick and nearly unbroken, pierced by only small windows”——半圆拱与筒形拱既向下又向外推力，故墙须厚、窗须小。B 正确。A、C 原文未提及为原因；D 与原文相反，罗马式屋顶同样沉重。

questions.stem: The word "ponderous" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: heavy
expensive
curved
ancient
questions.explain: ponderous ＝ 笨重的、沉重的，与 heavy 同义。原文说罗马式建筑者被迫依赖「ponderous walls（笨重的墙）」，与前文 thick walls 一致。B、C、D 均不符。

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, one advantage of the pointed arch over the semicircular arch is that the pointed arch
options: was an entirely original invention of Gothic masons
could span far wider openings than any earlier arch
could be given the same height regardless of the width it spanned
eliminated the need for windows in the outer walls
questions.explain: 原文：“a pointed arch, by contrast, can be made steeper or shallower independently of its span, giving builders the freedom to bring arches of unequal width to a common level”——尖拱高度可独立于跨度，从而使不同宽度的拱达到同一高度。C 正确。A 与「borrowed from earlier Islamic precedents」相反；B 原文未做跨度更大的比较；D 与本段无关。

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the essential information in the highlighted sentence in paragraph 2? Incorrect choices change the meaning or leave out essential information.
questions.highlight: More important still was the way the pointed arch handled thrust: because its sides rise more steeply toward the apex, the force it transmits is directed more nearly straight downward, reducing the sideways push that had obliged Romanesque builders to rely on such ponderous walls.
options: The pointed arch mattered most because its steeper sides sent force more straight down, lessening the sideways push that had forced Romanesque builders to use heavy walls.
The pointed arch was important mainly because its steep sides made it taller than the semicircular arch used in Romanesque churches.
Romanesque builders used heavy walls because they had not yet learned to build arches with steeply rising sides.
By directing all of a roof's weight sideways, the pointed arch removed the need for the thick walls of earlier churches.
questions.explain: 原句核心：尖拱最重要之处在于陡峭的拱腰把力更接近竖直向下传导，从而减小侧推力，使罗马式那种笨重厚墙不再必需。A 完整保留。B 只谈高度、漏掉推力这一关键；C 因果颠倒且非原句主旨；D 说「向侧面导出全部重量」与原句「向下」完全相反。

questions.stem: The word "intervening" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
options: decorative
in-between
collapsing
reinforced
questions.explain: intervening ＝ 位于其间的。原文「the intervening spaces, or webs」指肋架之间的空隙，故 in-between（其间的）最贴切。其余选项与「之间」之义无关。

questions.stem: Look at the four squares [■] in paragraph 3 that indicate where the following sentence could be added. Where would the sentence best fit?
questions.insert_sentence: The wall itself, in other words, no longer needed to be thick or continuous to hold the building up.
options: 方块 ①
方块 ②
方块 ③
方块 ④
questions.explain: 待插句用「in other words」重述前句「the flying buttress relieved the walls of their structural burden almost entirely（飞扶壁几乎完全卸去墙体的承重任务）」，并顺势引出下一句「Freed in this way, the wall … could be thinned」。故应放在第③个方块（该句与「Freed in this way」之间）。放①②太早（飞扶壁尚未介绍完），放④则打断 Beauvais 例证。

questions.stem: The word "this" in paragraph 4 (in the phrase "understood this glazing") refers to
options: the thick walls of Romanesque churches
the stained glass that filled the freed walls
the ribbed vault of the ceiling
the theological writings of Abbot Suger
questions.explain: 该句前半为「The walls … were filled with stained glass on a scale without precedent, and contemporaries understood this glazing as far more than decoration」——this glazing 回指前文刚提到的 stained glass（安装彩色玻璃这件事）。B 正确。A、C、D 均非 glazing 所指。

questions.stem: Why does the author discuss Abbot Suger in paragraph 4?
options: To identify the engineer who first calculated the thrust of the pointed arch
To show that a contemporary understood stained-glass light as a means of turning the mind toward the divine
To argue that ordinary worshipers fully grasped the theology of light
To explain why the collapse at Beauvais occurred
questions.explain: 原文借 Suger 说明当时人如何理解彩窗之光：「the colored light … could lift the mind from the material world toward the divine」，即把光当作通向神圣的媒介。B 正确。A 混淆工程与神学；C 与原文「Whether or not the ordinary worshiper grasped these … associations」（未必理解）相反；D 与 Suger 无关。

questions.stem: According to paragraph 5, all of the following help explain why medieval cathedrals were difficult to complete EXCEPT:
options: Construction could span a century or more and outlast several master masons.
Funding came from an unstable mix of sources that could be interrupted.
A change of master mason could alter a building's design partway through.
The lodges refused to share geometric knowledge with any patron who paid for the work.
questions.explain: A、B、C 均为原文明述的困难：工期逾百年、资金来源脆弱可中断、换主匠会改设计。D 是编造——原文只说石匠行会「guarded the geometric knowledge on which their trade depended（守护本行所依赖的几何知识）」，并未说「拒绝向出资者分享」这一具体情节，属无据推衍，故 EXCEPT 选 D。

questions.stem: An introductory sentence for a brief summary of the passage is provided below. Complete the summary by selecting the THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas in the passage.
questions.intro_sentence: Gothic cathedrals arose from structural innovations that redistributed a building's weight and allowed its walls to be replaced by glass.
options: The pointed arch, ribbed vault, and flying buttress together channeled the roof's forces to concentrated points and outside supports, freeing the walls from their load-bearing role.
With the walls no longer needed for support, they could be filled with vast stained-glass windows whose light was understood both as a path to the divine and as a way of teaching scripture.
Building a cathedral demanded enormous, sustained resources, so that funding, the mobility of masons' lodges, and construction times of a century or more all shaped the finished work.
The Romanesque style disappeared entirely from Europe within a few years of the rebuilding of Saint-Denis in the 1140s.
The collapse of the choir vault at Beauvais in 1284 proved that the flying buttress was an unworkable idea that later builders abandoned.
Stained-glass windows were valued chiefly because they kept cathedral interiors cool and protected worshipers from the weather.
questions.explain: ①尖拱—肋架拱顶—飞扶壁三者协同重新分配受力、解放墙体（第2、3段主旨）；②墙体解放后被巨大彩窗取代，光兼具通神与教化之义（第4段主旨）；③大教堂是耗时逾百年、资金脆弱、行会流动的浩大社会工程（第5段主旨）。干扰项：④原文只说 Gothic 自 Île-de-France 传播，未称罗马式「几年内彻底消失」；⑤Beauvais 坍塌是说建造者逼近极限，并未否定飞扶壁、更未被放弃；⑥「保持凉爽、遮风避雨」为编造，原文强调的是象征意义与叙事教化。
